title: How NRIs Can Invest in Indian Stocks and Mutual Funds Through NRE Accounts
excerpt: A step-by-step guide to investing in Indian markets from abroad, including account types, KYC requirements, tax implications, and platform options for 2026.
body:
• NRIs can invest in Indian stocks and mutual funds through NRE (Non-Resident External) or NRO (Non-Resident Ordinary) bank accounts under FEMA regulations
  • NRE accounts allow full repatriation of principal and earnings, while NRO accounts limit repatriation to $1 million per financial year
  • KYC completion, including PAN card, passport, and FATCA declaration, is mandatory before investing
  • US- and Canada-based NRIs face additional restrictions as some fund houses are not FATCA/CRS compliant
  • NRI investments in Indian mutual funds have grown to nearly $30 billion, reflecting rising global confidence in Indian markets

For NRIs looking to invest in India's growing financial markets, the process has become increasingly accessible, though it requires navigating specific regulatory requirements. Under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), NRIs, OCIs, and PIOs are all eligible to invest in Indian stocks and mutual funds — but they must do so through designated rupee-denominated accounts.

Choosing the Right Account: NRE vs. NRO

The first decision NRIs face is whether to open an NRE or NRO account, as Indian mutual fund companies and brokerages cannot accept foreign-currency investments directly.

An NRE (Non-Resident External) account is designed for depositing overseas earnings in India. Its key advantage is full repatriation — both principal and interest can be transferred back to the NRI's country of residence without restrictions. Interest earned in an NRE account is also exempt from Indian income tax.

An NRO (Non-Resident Ordinary) account is used for income earned within India, such as rent, dividends, or salary. While NRIs can invest from NRO accounts, repatriation is capped at $1 million per financial year, and interest earned is subject to Indian taxation.

The choice between the two depends on the source of funds and long-term financial goals. NRIs investing overseas earnings and wanting the flexibility to repatriate freely should generally opt for an NRE account.

Step-by-Step Investment Process

Once the account type is decided, here is the process:

1. Complete KYC (Know Your Customer): SEBI mandates KYC verification for all investors. NRIs need to submit a passport, PAN card, overseas address proof, a recent photograph, and a FATCA (Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act) declaration. Most asset management companies currently require offline KYC, meaning NRIs may need to be physically present in India for verification, though SEBI is working on enabling digital verification with video and geolocation tagging.

2. Open an NRE or NRO Account: Link the bank account to the investment platform. All transactions for a particular mutual fund must be routed through the same NRE or NRO account.

3. Select an Investment Platform: Options include AMC websites and apps (SBI Mutual Fund, ICICI Prudential, HDFC, Kotak), registrar platforms (myCAMS, KFintech), MF Central, BSE STAR MF, NSE platforms, or online platforms like Kuvera and Groww. NRIs can also invest through AMFI-registered distributors or financial advisors.

4. Power of Attorney Option: NRIs who cannot manage investments directly can appoint a trusted representative in India through a Power of Attorney (PoA). The PoA holder must also be KYC compliant.

Key Restrictions for US and Canada NRIs

NRIs based in the United States and Canada face additional hurdles. Some AMCs restrict investments from these countries because they may not be FATCA or CRS (Common Reporting Standard) compliant. This means not all mutual fund schemes are available to US- and Canada-based NRIs, and investors should verify fund house eligibility before committing capital.

"Over the years, NRI investments in Indian mutual funds grew to almost $30 billion. This reflects growing global confidence in Indian financial instruments."

— Kotak Bank

Tax Implications and Redemption

Tax treatment differs by account type and holding period. Short-term capital gains on equity mutual funds (held less than one year) are taxed at 15%, while long-term gains above Rs 1 lakh are taxed at 10%. For debt mutual funds, gains are added to income and taxed at the applicable slab rate. TDS (Tax Deducted at Source) is automatically deducted on redemption proceeds for NRI investors.

To redeem mutual fund units, NRIs submit a redemption request either at the AMC office or online. Proceeds are credited to the linked NRE or NRO account after applicable tax deductions. NRIs can also claim tax treaty benefits under the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) between India and their country of residence.

Getting Started

The process may seem complex, but once KYC and account setup are complete, investing becomes straightforward. NRIs should start by checking whether their chosen fund house accepts investments from their country of residence, complete KYC during their next India visit if digital options are not available, and consult a tax advisor familiar with both Indian and local tax obligations.
